subscribe.honestTitle: What this is, and what it is not
subscribe.honestModel: Alerts fire on our estimate for your point, not on an official CPCB reading of that exact spot.
subscribe.honestWindow: The CPCB bands are defined on 24-hour averages. We compare them against an hourly estimate, so an alert is a heads-up, not an official classification.
subscribe.honestPrivacy: Your address is stored only to send these alerts, and every email contains a one-click unsubscribe.
subscribe.honestRate: At most one email per crossing. There is no daily summary.

crosscheck.title: Independent check
crosscheck.explainer: Two different measurements of the same air. Ours is anchored to the nearest CPCB monitor, so it can catch a pocket of pollution a regional grid smooths away; CAMS is a satellite-and-model average over tens of kilometres. A gap is normal — a large one usually means your street is dirtier than the regional average, not that the number is wrong.
crosscheck.notAReading: This is a model, not a monitor at your address.
crosscheck.unavailable: No independent reading available right now.
crosscheck.dustNote: Delhi's dust season is strong right now, so the aerosol reading includes dust — it is not fire smoke.

versions.title: Every model version we kept
versions.explainer: Each retrain is kept, not overwritten, so a change in accuracy is visible rather than silent. A version marked pruned still lists the commit that produced it, so the model can be recovered from history. MAE is measured at training time on that version's own holdout.

algo.title: Algorithm, data and accuracy
algo.intro: Everything about how the number is produced: the algorithm, the pipeline it runs, the features it reads, the data it was trained on, and the measured accuracy of each. Every figure here is read from the API and updates when the model is retrained.

pipeline.title: Find the nearest monitor
pipeline.body: The closest CPCB station to the point you selected, with its most recent reading and its history. If nothing is within range the API says so rather than guessing.

pipeline.title: Read the weather
pipeline.body: Hourly temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, pressure, rainfall and solar radiation at your coordinates. Wind direction matters most: pollution travels downwind from a source.

pipeline.title: Predict the change, not the level
pipeline.body: The model learns the residual between the current and previous station reading, so its job is only to work out the correction. Repeating the last reading is therefore built into the model as the thing it has to beat.

pipeline.title: Take three quantiles
pipeline.body: Separate models are trained for the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile. The median becomes the estimate and the outer two describe the spread before calibration.

pipeline.title: Calibrate the interval
pipeline.body: Raw quantile models under-cover during sharp swings. A conformal radius fitted on held-out data widens the interval until it actually contains the truth about 80% of the time.

pipeline.title: Correct for distance
pipeline.body: A station far away says less about your street, so the correction shrinks toward the anchor and the interval is widened rather than quietly reported as if it were precise.

algo.accuracyNote: Two protocols, because they answer different questions. Future hours asks whether a known station can be predicted an hour ahead. Unseen station holds out whole stations, which is the harder and more relevant test for a new locality - and the row shown in amber is the one to trust when you are far from a monitor. The baseline is the honest alternative to any model: repeat the last reading. Everything here is a conservative lower bound, because the recorded evaluation scores a model fitted on the training split while the shipped model is refitted on all of it.
algo.categoriesNote: Official CPCB bands, applied to hourly values as a deliberate simplification.
